title_options: Two Writers, One Memory: What Concurrent Agent Writes Actually Lose (2026)
Concurrent Agent Memory Writes: Which Pattern Silently Overwrote the Newer Fact
Four Writers, One SQLite Memory Table: Delete-Then-Insert Lost 365-503 of 1,000 Writes
presentation.title_rationale: The reader's problem is a silent overwrite when more than one process writes the same memory table, so the title names the situation (two writers, one memory) and promises exactly what the experiment delivers: a measurement of what is actually lost, not a general warning that concurrency is hard. The measured patterns and their numbers are in the description and introduction rather than pushed into the headline.
presentation.visual_purpose: Horizontal bar chart of lost-update writes per 1,000 attempts for the four write patterns, values read directly from the published raw/summary.csv ranges across three repeats and three locking configurations. It explains the article's central contrast in one look: the guarded UPSERT at zero against the delete-then-insert replace at 365-503. Scope is printed on the image: four processes, 25 keys, one 2-vCPU host, local fixture, not vendor data.

claims.note: Title and description summarise this article's own measured matrix (1000 attempts per cell over 25 keys, 365-503 lost-update writes for the delete-then-insert pattern); the figures are restated in the results table and traced to raw/summary.csv, and no vendor, traffic or ranking claim is made.
Failure scenario is stated as a hypothetical team situation, not an observed incident; the 'step 40' and 'step 12' values are illustrative step numbers, not measured data.

Describes the experiment this article actually ran: four processes, 1000 attempts per cell, 25 keys, four patterns, three configurations, three repeats, stdlib sqlite3 only; the run record and raw per-write traces are the cited artifact.
